episodes.213173: A strong upper trough moved east toward the area that helped to produce severe thundertorms over a good portion of the CWA. Flooding also occurred in parts of the area.
episodes.213182: An upper level disturbance touched off scattered showers and thunderstorms, one of which turned severe in coastal NC.
episodes.213187: Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time. Thunderstorms produced a few tornadoes on the evening of June 26th.
episodes.213239: A line of thunderstorms moved through north central and northeast South Dakota late on June 27 into the early morning of June 28, generating isolated pockets of high winds. A personal weather station in northeast Aberdeen and the South Dakota State University mesonet station seven miles south of Claremont both recorded peak wind gusts of 70 mph.
episodes.213262: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.||In addition, locally repeated heavy rainfall produced some urban flash flooding in Rock Valley.
episodes.213301: A nearly stationary boundary hovered over central Ohio, northern West Virginia, and southern Pennsylvania on June 27th and 28th, but eventually sank south of the area early on the morning of the 29th. ||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms continued to develop along and south of the front, depositing one to three inches of rain across much of the area. While the heaviest rain amounts fell in the southern coal fields, soils to the north had already been compromised by prior rounds of precipitation. Thus, an inch to an inch-and-a-half of rain was enough to spawn some flooding on roads in Harrison, Barbour, and Randolph counties.
episodes.213358: Lightning damaged two homes in North Carolina during the evening hours.
episodes.213538: Early in the afternoon June 28th, a cluster of strong storms moved into northeast Iowa, producing very heavy rain, and strong winds gusts around 50 mph. As this cluster of storms dropped southeast, it became a single severe storm as it moved closer to Clinton County Iowa. Large hail and damaging winds occurs in this last portion of the storm before it dissipated as it moved farther into Illinois.
episodes.213646: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain across portions of Pickett and Fentress counties on June 28, 2026. An estimated five to seven inches fell across the area from Byrdstown to Jamestown which caused flash flooding. The Wolf River near Byrdstown crested to 15.29 inches, the second highest crest of record. Roadways along the river and nearby creeks were inundated with water and rendered impassable. One home in Byrdstown also reported being inundated with water.
episodes.213696: Another round of thunderstorms occurred during the late afternoon and early evening hours of June 27th. These thunderstorms produced quarter sized hail in a few locations.
episodes.213707: Thunderstorms developed through the evening hours as an upper level low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.213940: During the early morning hours of June 28, 2026, a mesoscale convective system (MCS) tracked across southeast South Dakota and far northeast Nebraska, producing damaging wind gusts. At 3:01 AM CST, a personal weather station 7 miles north of Crofton, Nebraska, measured a peak wind gust of 63 mph. The complex gradually decayed as it moved eastward, leaving this as the lone report from the area.
episodes.214161: Troughing was evident over the western CONUS on the 28th, and west Texas and southeast New Mexico were under southwesterly flow aloft. Pulses within this flow, coupled with upslope flow and surface convergence on a weak dryline, yielded shower and thunderstorm development starting in the higher terrain and spreading across much of the area. A few thunderstorms managed to produce severe downburst winds.
episodes.214185: A warm and moist environment set up across Eastern North Carolina during the afternoon hours of June Twenty-Eighth. At the same time the seabreeze combined with a surface trough across the Coastal Plain and an incoming cold front to become the focus of scattered shower and thunderstorm activity during the afternoon and evening hours. With this favorable environment in place, a few of these storms became strong to severe in nature bringing a strong and damaging wind threat to the Neuse and Bay Rivers, southern Pamlico Sound, and along the coastal waters south of Ocracoke Island.
episodes.214972: A warm front lifted across North Dakota while strong southerly surface flow increased temperatures and dew points over the region. As a surface trough tracked to the east, storms developed in eastern Montana and moved into western North Dakota during the evening. Storms quickly formed a line as they continued moving east-northeast, with powerful wind gusts the primary hazard across western and portions of central North Dakota. A tornado occurred approximately 7 miles north-northeast of Belfield in Billings County. The track was less than one mile long and wind speeds were estimated up to 90 mph, leading to an EF-1 rating. Damaging wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph were common across the area as storms moved through. The most significant damage occurred in a neighborhood west of Williston. The Emergency Manager reported debris in a southwest to northeast orientation, consistent with straight line winds. Notable damage includes two homes with roofs uplifted and partially blown off. Other damage includes sheds, enclosed trailers, and campers damaged or destroyed. Some tree damage was also noted. Damage is consistent with wind speeds around 95 mph.
episodes.215026: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted much of western SD and the eastern Plains. Biggest threat was large hail which was confirmed by numerous chaser reports. Damaging wind gusts were also measured by SD mesonet stations and personal weather stations across the area.
episodes.215124: An area of decaying showers produced localized winds which gusted as high as 50 mph across parts of southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon of June 28th.
episodes.215257: A deep mid-level trough over the northwestern U.S. ejected a leading wave into the northern High Plains early on June 28. An increasing low level jet of 45 to 60 knots developed through the Central Plains with a terminus over southeast South Dakota. The source airmass exhibited up to 3000-4000 J/kg elevated CAPE, significant DCAPE, and 40 to 50 knots of deep-layer effective shear. Storms intensified and organized into short bowing segments with swaths of damaging winds across southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota. On the more exposed southern periphery of convection, briefly stronger updrafts brought areas of hail as large as ping-pong balls across northwest Iowa.

episodes.215314: Scattered thunderstorms developed over the northern panhandle and far southern South Dakota during the early evening hours of June 27th. As this activity tracked east into the late evening and early overnight hours, hail up to the size of golf balls and wind gusts up to 79 MPH were reported.
episodes.215316: A few thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across the South Carolina Piedmont during the afternoon. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.215332: An MCS moved out of Kentucky into East Tennessee during the early morning hours of June 28th. This laid out a boundary that acted as a focus for additional shower and thunderstorm development through the late morning hours, resulting in training storms across the central Tennessee valley and numerous reports of flooding.
episodes.215493: Mainly zonal flow aloft with embedded low amplitude perturbations resulted in scattered thunderstorm development across central Virginia with heavy rainfall and flash flooding.
episodes.215707: A shortwave embedded in a weakness in an upper ridge led to a MCS developing in the Tennessee Valley that moved into the forecast area late afternoon. While this system was decaying as it reached the area, it produced severe wind gusts in Lancaster, SC.
episodes.215735: Moderate to strong instability south of a frontal boundary draped across the northern Florida peninsula supported afternoon convection that produced a tornado near Fort Myers in Lee County.
episodes.215822: Slow moving thunderstorms resulted in 2-3 inches of rain over portions of eastern Allegheny County, PA in the afternoon on the 28th. Flash flooding lead to road closures along Thompson Run Road, Rodi Road and Route 48.
episodes.215830: On June 28th a weak upper level shortwave interacted with modest shear and CAPE to create enough energy to trigger a few isolated thunderstorms.  One area of storms across central Maine, grew stronger enough for isolated severe hail and wind gusts.
episodes.215973: Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas. Rainfall totals for the weekend ended up in an area wide 2-4 inches with swaths of 6-10+ inches!!  Unfortunately 3 fatalities were confirmed due to flooding in Madison County, KY, and 1 fatality indirectly related to the flooding occurred on Floyds Fork in Jefferson County, KY.
